notes.text: The way which is desert — There were two ways from Jerusalem to Gaza, one desert, the other through a more populous country.

An eunuch — Chief officers were anciently called eunuchs, though not always literally such; because such used to be chief ministers in the eastern courts. Candace, queen of the Ethiopians - So all the queens of Ethiopia were called.

Sitting in his chariot, he read the Prophet Isaiah — God meeteth those that remember him in his ways. It is good to read, hear, seek information even in a journey. Why should we not redeem all our time?

And Philip running to him, said, Understandest thou what thou readest? — He did not begin about the weather, news, or the like. In speaking for God, we may frequently come to the point at once, without circumlocution.
He desired Philip to come up and sit with him — Such was his modesty, and thirst after instruction.

The portion of Scripture — By reading that very chapter, the fifty-third of Isaiah, many Jews, yea, and atheists, have been converted. Some of them history records. God knoweth them all. Isaiah liii, 7

In his humiliation his judgment was taken away — That is, when he was a man, he had no justice shown him. To take away a person's judgment, is a proverbial phrase for oppressing him. And who shall declare, or count his generation - That is, who can number his seed, Isaiah liii, 10; which he hath purchased by laying down his life?

And as they went on the way they came to a certain water — Thus, even the circumstances of the journey were under the direction of God. The kingdom of God suits itself to external circumstances, without any violence, as air yields to all bodies, and yet pervades all. What hindereth me to be baptized? - Probably he had been circumcised: otherwise Cornelius would not have been the first fruits of the Gentiles.
And they both went down — Out of the chariot. It does not follow that he was baptized by immersion. The text neither affirms nor intimates any thing concerning it.
The Spirit of the Lord caught away Philip — Carried him away with a miraculous swiftness, without any action or labour of his own. This had befallen several of the prophets.
But Philip was found at Azotus — Probably none saw him, from his leaving the eunuch, till he was there.

glossa.text: *And an angel.* After the return of the apostles, the history is woven concerning Philip. *To the way,* etc. For the way goes down, and by the way one goes down, from the nature of the place.

*An Ethiopian.* By nature and by desert. For an Ethiopian is dark. Whence: *Ethiopia shall prevent her hands to God ((Psal. LXVII))*.

*A man of power,* etc. ((BEDA.)) The queen of the Ethiopians sending her treasurer before her, etc., *as far as, Hearken, O daughter, and see, and incline thy ear ((Psal. XLIV))*, etc.

*Of queen Candace.* It was the custom of that region to be ruled by women, and that they should be called Candaces.

*He was returning.* He was beginning to return, reading Isaias. Wherever in the New Testament the beginning of salvation is related, the testimony is taken from Isaias, who is interpreted *the salvation of the Lord.*
*Thinkest thou that thou understandest,* etc. ((RAB.)) They know each other's tongues, either through the learning of the eunuch or through the spirit of Philip.
*How,* etc. Here he reproves the boldness of those who think that they understand Holy Scripture without a teacher.

*In humility. ((BEDA.))* For indeed the judge of all found not the truth of judgment, but without any fault of his own, by the sedition of the Jews and by the voice of Pilate, he was condemned.

*Humility. ((RAB.))* By the passion in which *he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death ((Philip. II))*.

 *He shall be taken away.* The second man from heaven, heavenly, separated by holiness from earthly things, or, he shall pass from life into death.

*He opened. ((RAB.))* He opened the treasure of knowledge. Or he opened his mouth, that the Spirit might speak in him, according to that: *Open wide thy mouth, and I will fill it ((Psal. LXXX))*.

Mystically, Philip opened the mouth of the Church, that from this he whom before they knew not might be preached to the Gentiles.

*He preached the Gospel.* He solves the question of him that asked: *Of whom did the prophet speak?* But he shows that it was prophesied of Jesus.
*To a certain water.* For to this the preaching had led, that he should need water, the things which he had heard on the way concerning baptism.

*If thou believest. ((RAB.))* He was not ignorant of his faith, but wished an open confession, that to those who are to baptize and to those who are to be baptized an example might be given of questioning and of confessing.
*The Spirit of the Lord. ((RAB.))* Or the Spirit rushed upon him mightily, as also upon the apostles, etc., *as far as* upon whom the Spirit had descended?

*He was found.* By men, he who in his rapture was not found, because he walked in the wilderness, or with exceeding swiftness.

*Caesarea. ((BEDA.))* He means the Caesarea of Palestine, where below he is described to have had a house, which is shown even to this day, and also the chamber of his four daughters, virgins that prophesied.

notes.text: Great congregation — In the universal church, of Jews and Gentiles.

Satisfied — This is doubtless to be understood, of those spiritual blessings, that grace and peace, and comfort, which all believing souls have in the sense of God's love, the pardon of their sins, and the influences of God's spirit. Seek him - That seek his favour. Your heart - He speaks of the same persons still, though there be a change from the third to the second person, as is usual in these poetical books. For ever - Your comfort shall not be short and transitory, as worldly comforts are, but everlasting.

The world — All nations from one end of the world to the other. So this is an evident prophecy of the calling of the Gentiles, and a clear proof, that this psalm immediately speaks of Christ; to whom alone, this and divers other passages of it, belong. Remember - They shall remember their former wickedness with grief and shame, and fear; particularly in worshiping dead and impotent idols. They shall remember their great and manifold obligation to God, which they had quite forgotten, his patience in sparing them so long, in the midst of all their impieties, and in giving his son for them: they shall remember the gracious words and glorious works of Christ, what he did, and suffered for them; which possibly divers of them had been eye and ear-witnesses of. The Lord - Into the only true God, and unto Jesus Christ, to whom this name of Jehovah is often ascribed in scripture.
For — This is added as a reason, why the Gentiles should be converted, because God is not only God and the Lord of the Jews, but also of the Gentiles, and of all nations.

Fat — Kings and princes, and the great men of the world. Shall eat - Shall feed upon the bread of life, Christ and all his benefits. Worship - This is added to shew what kind of eating he spoke of. Go down - That is, all mankind, for none can escape death.

A seed — Christ shall not want a seed or posterity, for though the Jewish nation will generally reject him, the Gentiles shall come in their stead. A generation - That believing seed shall be reputed both by God and men, The generation, or people of the Lord, as the Jews formerly were.

They — The seed last mentioned. Come - From Judea and Jerusalem (from whence the gospel was first to go forth) to the Gentile world, to the several parts whereof the apostles went upon this errand. His - God's righteousness: his wonderful grace and mercy unto mankind, in giving them Christ and the gospel; for righteousness is often put for mercy or kindness. Unto - Unto succeeding generations. Whereby David gives us a key to understand this psalm, and teaches us that he speaks not here of himself, but of things which were to be done in after-ages, even of the spreading of the gospel among the Gentiles, in the time of the New Testament. That he - They shall declare that this is the work of God, and not of man. David extolls the goodness of God as his shepherd, and expresses his confidence in him, ver. 1-6. A psalm of David.

glossa.text: *With thee is my praise in a great church,* etc. ((ID.)) He places his praise with God, who teaches that there be no presuming in man.

*They shall praise the Lord that seek him: they shall live.* ((ID.)) The poor are rich in God: therefore poor, because they praise God that they may seek him, and he himself is the riches of the poor. *Their hearts shall remember for ever and ever, and shall be converted to the Lord.* ((ID.)) Because he is the food of the heart.

*They have eaten and have adored.* ((ID.)) Let not the dispenser forbid to eat, but let him warn the exactor to fear. *In his sight shall they fall.* ((CASS.)) The Church receives both, but he himself sees and discerns.

*It shall be shewn,* etc. ((ID.)) Or to the angels, who offer the prayers of men to God, not for instruction, but for ministry.

((CASS.)) Note that the psalms of the passion end in the great hope of Christians, that it may be known that salvation is from the passion.

notes.text: Let us love one another — From the doctrine he has just been defending he draws this exhortation. It is by the Spirit that the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts. Everyone that truly loveth God and his neighbour is born of God.

God is love — This little sentence brought St. John more sweetness, even in the time he was writing it, than the whole world can bring. God is often styled holy, righteous, wise; but not holiness, righteousness, or wisdom in the abstract, as he is said to be love; intimating that this is his darling, his reigning attribute, the attribute that sheds an amiable glory on all his other perfections.
If we love one another, God abideth in us — This is treated of, 1 John iv, 13-16. And his love is perfected - Has its full effect. In us - This is treated of, 1 John iv, 17-19.

And in consequence of this we have seen and testify that the Father sent the Son — These are the foundation and the criteria of our abiding in God and God in us, the communion of the Spirit, and the confession of the Son.
Whosoever shall, from a principle of loving faith, openly confess in the face of all opposition and danger, that Jesus is the Son of God, God abideth in him.
And we know and believe — By the same Spirit, the love that God hath to us.

Hereby — That is, by this communion with God. Is our love made perfect; that we may - That is, so that we shall have boldness in the day of judgment - When all the stout-hearted shall tremble. Because as he - Christ. Is - All love. So are we - Who are fathers in Christ, even in this world.

There is no fear in love — No slavish fear can be where love reigns. But perfect, adult love casteth out slavish fear: because such fear hath torment - And so is inconsistent with the happiness of love. A natural man has neither fear nor love; one that is awakened, fear without love; a babe in Christ, love and fear; a father in Christ, love without fear.
We love him, because he first loved us — This is the sum of all religion, the genuine model of Christianity. None can say more: why should any one say less, or less intelligibly?
Whom he hath seen — Who is daily presented to his senses, to raise his esteem, and move his kindness or compassion toward him.

And this commandment have we from him — Both God and his opinions or mode of worship be, purely because he is the child, and bears the image, of God. Bigotry is properly the want of this pure and universal love. A bigot only loves those who embrace his opinions, and receives his way of worship; and he loves them for that, and not for Christ's sake.

glossa.text: *Dearly beloved, let us love one another.* He has commended charity in many ways, now he comes to its singular praise, wherein we ought most of all to hear him, namely: *He that loveth is born of God and knoweth God, because God is charity.* He had said: *Charity is of God;* here he has added further: *God is charity.*

*Because God is charity.* Charity does not differ in God, since he is called both just and justice, as also loving and love, because he is not called just by a transferred name from justice, nor loving by love, as though he had a justice or a love distinct from himself, but because he is his own justice and love.

*In this hath appeared.* By proving that God is charity and that he loves us, he wished to lead us on by his own example, that we should love one another and come to the knowledge of him. As God did not wait for us to love him, so let us not wait for others to love us, but let us love first. The love of the Father has been proved, because he sent the Son: the love of the Son appeared in this, that he died for us whom he loved beforehand.

*Not as though we had loved God.* We did not love first, so that he should love us as though by the merit of our love, but he himself loved us first, that with his grace going before we should love him.

*And we ought to love one another.* Love, and do what thou wilt. Whether thou art silent, be silent in love: whether thou criest out, cry out in love. From this root nothing can come forth except good.

*No man hath seen God at any time. ((BEDA.))* As those visible things known to the senses of the body are seen, so God is not seen, etc., *as far as* while we are still pilgrims in the body, let us love one another, etc.

*In this we know.* Whence shall we know whether we have the Spirit of God? Question thine own bowels: if they are full of charity, thou hast the Spirit of God. *Because we abide in him.* God abides in us, and we in him, and therefore let no one despair of salvation, because although the diseases of crimes weigh us down, the physician who saves is almighty. Let us rejoice in hope, that we may come to the reality.

*And we have known.* We have seen and bear witness that God sent his Son, and we have known for what cause he did this: not because he had need, not because he owed anything, but out of charity alone. Though he had an only Son, he willed not that he should be one alone, but that he might have brethren, and he adopted for him those who should possess eternal life with him.
*Fear is not in charity.* In that charity, namely, which in imitation of the divine goodness does good even to enemies, there is no fear.

notes.text: I am the true vine — So the true bread, Chap. vi, 32; that is, the most excellent.

Everyone that beareth fruit, he purifieth — by obeying the truth, 1 Pet. i, 22; and by inward or outward sufferings, Heb. xii, 10, 11. So purity and fruitfulness help each other. That it may bear more fruit - For this is one of the noblest rewards God can bestow on former acts of obedience, to make us yet more holy, and fit for farther and more eminent service.
Ye are clean — All of you, to whom I now speak, are purged from the guilt and power of sin; by the word - Which, applied by the Spirit, is the grand instrument of purifying the soul.
Abide in me — Ye who are now pure by living faith, producing all holiness; by which alone ye can be in me.
I am the vine, ye are the branches — Our Lord in this whole passage speaks of no branches but such as are, or at least were once, united to him by living faith.

If any one abide not in me — By living faith; not by Church communion only. He may thus abide in Christ, and be withered all the time, and cast into the fire at last. He is cast out - Of the vineyard, the invisible Church. Therefore he was in it once.
If ye abide in me, ye shall ask — Prayers themselves are a fruit of faith, and they produce more fruit.
So shall ye be my disciples — Worthy of the name. To be a disciple of Christ is both the foundation and height of Christianity.

glossa.text: *I am the true vine.* And you ought to follow me as I go before to the passion, because I am the vine, that is, your head, of the same nature with you, that in me human nature may be able to bear fruit. *And the Father,* etc. I too am the husbandman together with the Father, because I am the cleanser of the branches, which is the office of the husbandman, not of the vine, who also makes the branches workmen, though not out of what is their own, nor through them, but through myself.
*Because of the word,* etc. He does not say: because of the water of baptism, because that also, without the word, is water only; through the word it becomes a sacrament.

*I am,* etc. He who reckons that he bears fruit of himself is not in the vine. Whence, with a repetition and an explanation of what went before, he adds: *I am the vine, you the branches.* Cleaving to me as to a vine. *He that abideth in me.* And therefore whosoever (not you only) abides in me by believing, by obeying, by persevering. *And I in him.* By enlightening, by succouring, by giving perseverance. *He beareth.* And although according to the man Christ is the vine. yet he would not give this grace to the branches unless he were also God.
*If any one.* Shoots that have been cut off are of less worth than other woods, because they are appointed to no uses but the fire; they are either in the vine or in the fire.

*And the words.* The words of God are then said to abide in us, when we do the things he commands and love the things he promises. But he who does not do this touches, he does not cleave; and therefore they are not to him for a benefit but for a testimony of damnation. *You shall ask.* If a faithful man asks anything and it is not done, he does not ask that which the mansion in him has, nor that which his words which are in him have, but that which cupidity and the infirmity of the flesh have.

*In this is glorified,* etc. He who abides in me bears much fruit, which is from the grace of God, and so it is his glory, not man's; and this is: *In this,* etc. *That you bring forth very much fruit.* Just as he shows not an equality of our nature and his, but the grace by which he is Mediator; for the Father loves us, but in the Son. *That you may become.* How? If you shall have loved me. From what love? From the observance of the precepts. If you shall have loved me as the Father loved me, not as much. For an equality is not noted, but a likeness giving them eternal eternity.

echoes.text: Neither let the foreigner, who has joined himself to Yahweh, speak, saying, “Yahweh will surely separate me from his people”; neither let the eunuch say, “Behold, I am a dry tree.” For thus says Yahweh, “To the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths, and choose the things that please me, and hold fast my covenant: to them I will give in my house and within my walls a memorial and a name better than of sons and of daughters; I will give them an everlasting name, […]
echoes.note: The Ethiopian 'eunuch' brought into the people of God figurally fulfills Isaiah's promise that the eunuch who keeps covenant will be given 'a name better than of sons and of daughters' within God's house. The correspondence is typological with strong thematic coherence (an excluded class welcomed); fittingly, the eunuch is reading the very scroll of Isaiah. Verbal volume is low, but the structural irony is pointed and the placement makes the allusion deliberate.

echoes.text: He who is emasculated by crushing or cutting shall not enter into Yahweh’s assembly.
echoes.note: The eunuch's prior exclusion is defined by the Torah's ruling that one 'wounded in the stones' shall not 'enter into the congregation of the LORD.' Luke's account quietly overturns this barrier; the coherence is high as the legal foil against which the eunuch's incorporation is read. No verbal borrowing, so the link is typological/figural.

echoes.text: Princes shall come out of Egypt. Ethiopia shall hurry to stretch out her hands to God.
echoes.note: An Ethiopian official coming to worship and returning home a believer answers the psalm's vision that 'Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God.' Thematic coherence is strong (Ethiopia turning to the true God) and the motif recurs in prophetic universalism; verbal volume is modest, making this a probable thematic allusion.

echoes.text: From beyond the rivers of Cush, my worshipers, even the daughter of my dispersed people, will bring my offering.
echoes.note: The eunuch as a worshiper coming 'from beyond the rivers of Ethiopia' to bring offering echoes Zephaniah's promise that 'from beyond the rivers of Ethiopia my suppliants... shall bring mine offering.' Recurrence with Psalm 68 strengthens the Ethiopia-to-Zion theme; volume is faint and the link is conceptual.

echoes.text: When the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon concerning Yahweh’s name, she came to prove him with hard questions. She came to Jerusalem with a very great train, with camels that bore spices, and very much gold, and precious stones; and when she had come to Solomon, she talked with him of all that was in her heart.
echoes.note: A high official of a southern queen ('Candace, queen of the Ethiopians,' steward of her treasure) journeying toward Jerusalem loosely recalls the Queen of Sheba's pilgrimage with her treasures to hear wisdom. Thematic coherence (foreign royalty seeking the God of Israel) is moderate; correspondence is associative, not verbal.

echoes.text: He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t open his mouth. As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is mute, so he didn’t open his mouth. He was taken away by oppression and judgment; and as for his generation, who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living and stricken for the disobedience of my people?
echoes.note: The scroll the eunuch reads is quoted verbatim from the Septuagint of the Suffering Servant: 'He was led as a sheep to the slaughter; as a lamb before his shearer is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth. In his humiliation his judgment was taken away...' Volume is maximal (sustained, explicit citation), and Philip's exposition makes the christological coherence the hinge of the pericope. This is the chapter's flagship quotation.

echoes.text: It will happen, as soon as I am gone from you, that the Spirit of Yahweh will carry you I don’t know where; and so when I come and tell Ahab, and he can’t find you, he will kill me. But I, your servant, have feared Yahweh from my youth.
echoes.note: After the baptism 'the Spirit of the Lord caught Philip away,' echoing the Elijah tradition in which 'the Spirit of the LORD shall carry thee whither I know not.' Volume is strong on the distinctive 'Spirit of the LORD carrying off' a prophet, recurrence within the Elijah/Elisha cycle is notable, and thematic coherence (a Spirit-driven prophetic figure transported) is high.

echoes.text: They said to him, “See now, there are with your servants fifty strong men. Please let them go and seek your master. Perhaps the Spirit of Yahweh has taken him up, and put him on some mountain, or into some valley. He said, “You shall not send them.”
echoes.note: Philip's sudden removal also recalls the sons of the prophets' fear that 'the Spirit of the LORD hath taken up [Elijah], and cast him upon some mountain.' Reinforces the Elijah-typology behind Philip's translation; volume and coherence parallel the 1 Kings 18 link, the two together making the prophetic-rapture allusion firm.

echoes.text: Then the Spirit lifted me up, and I heard behind me the voice of a great rushing, saying, Blessed be Yahweh’s glory from his place. I heard the noise of the wings of the living creatures as they touched one another, and the noise of the wheels beside them, even the noise of a great rushing. So the Spirit lifted me up, and took me away; and I went in bitterness, in the heat of my spirit; and the hand of Yahweh was strong on me.
echoes.note: The Spirit 'lifting up' and bearing away the prophet matches Ezekiel's experience that 'the Spirit took me up, and... carried me away.' Recurrence of Spirit-transport language across the prophets strengthens the motif; verbal volume here is moderate, the link best classed as a supporting echo to the Elijah allusions.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.id: The City of David and Old City, on the spurs above the Kidron Valley, c. 50 km from the Mediterranean. Pre-Israelite Jebus; named here as the seat of Adoni-Zedek, leader of the southern coalition.

places.name: Gaza
places.id: The southernmost of the five Philistine pentapolis cities, on the coastal plain c. 80 km SW of Jerusalem. The west-coast extreme of the southern campaign’s reach in v.41.

places.name: Ashdod
places.id: Tell Ashdod, c. 6 km inland from the Mediterranean. One of the five Philistine pentapolis cities; identified securely on the basis of toponymic continuity.

places.name: Ethiopia
places.id: In Greco-Roman usage, the kingdom of Kush / Meroe in the upper Nile (modern central Sudan), south of Egyptian Aswan. The Candace ('queen-mother') was the standard title of its rulers. Pin sits at Meroe.

places.name: Caesarea
places.id: On the Mediterranean coast c. 60 km northwest of Jerusalem, on the site of an earlier Hellenistic Strato's Tower. Rebuilt by Herod the Great as a deepwater harbor with concrete moles, an aqueduct from Mount Carmel, and a temple to Roma and Augustus. The administrative capital of Roman Judea/Palaestina from c. 6 A.D. Distinct from Caesarea Philippi (Banias) at the foot of Mount Hermon.

echoes.text: Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth,
echoes.note: The declaration 'God is love' distills the self-revelation of the LORD as abounding in steadfast love (hesed). John's identification of love with God's very being is the climactic theological development of the Sinai name-formula proclaiming the LORD merciful, gracious, and abounding in lovingkindness.

echoes.text: He said, “You cannot see my face, for man may not see me and live.”
echoes.note: 'No one has seen God at any time' echoes the LORD's word to Moses, 'you cannot see my face, for no one can see me and live.' John takes the unseeability of God as a premise and resolves it through mutual love: the invisible God is made manifest when believers love one another.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses, after the death of the two sons of Aaron, when they drew near before Yahweh, and died; and Yahweh said to Moses, “Tell Aaron your brother, not to come at all times into the Most Holy Place within the veil, before the mercy seat which is on the ark; lest he die: for I will appear in the cloud on the mercy seat. “Aaron shall come into the sanctuary with a young bull for a sin offering, and a ram for a burnt offering. He shall put on […]
echoes.note: The sending of the Son 'as the atoning sacrifice (propitiation) for our sins' draws on the Day of Atonement ritual, where the blood of the sin offering and the scapegoat effect expiation before the LORD at the mercy seat (hilasterion). John casts Christ as the means of atonement fulfilling the Levitical kapporet.

echoes.text: Surely he has borne our sickness, and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted. But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all. He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t […]
echoes.note: God sending his Son as the atoning sacrifice 'for our sins' echoes the Servant who bore our griefs and was made an offering for sin, the righteous one making many righteous. The vicarious, sin-bearing logic of the Servant Song informs John's account of love defined by the Son sent as propitiation.

echoes.text: Yahweh didn’t set his love on you, nor choose you, because you were more in number than any people; for you were the fewest of all peoples: but because Yahweh loves you, and because he desires to keep the oath which he swore to your fathers, Yahweh has brought you out with a mighty hand, and redeemed you out of the house of bondage, from the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt.
echoes.note: 'Not that we loved God, but that he loved us' restates the Deuteronomic ground of election: the LORD set his love on Israel not for any merit but because he loved them. The priority and gratuity of divine love that precedes any human response shapes John's theology of love originating wholly in God.

echoes.text: “When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt. They called to them, so they went from them. They sacrificed to the Baals, and burned incense to engraved images. Yet I taught Ephraim to walk. I took them by his arms; but they didn’t know that I healed them. I drew them with cords of a man, with ties of love; and I was to them like those who lift up the yoke on their necks; and I bent down to him and I fed him.
echoes.note: Hosea's portrait of God's parental love drawing Israel with cords of human kindness and bands of love grounds John's claim that love is of God and that God first loved us. The tender, initiating love of the LORD for his child stands behind the manifestation of God's love in sending the Son.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Let us love one another' rests on the Holiness Code command to love your neighbor as yourself. John universalizes and intensifies the neighbor-love command, grounding mutual love in the divine nature itself.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to you out of the midst of the fire: you heard the voice of words, but you saw no form; you only heard a voice.
echoes.note: At Horeb Israel heard a voice but saw no form, reinforcing the unseeability of God that John presupposes in 'no one has seen God at any time.' The Deuteronomic insistence that no visible form accompanied the theophany feeds the Johannine claim that God is known not by sight but by abiding love.

echoes.text: Jacob called the name of the place Peniel: for, he said, “I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved.”
echoes.note: Jacob's wonder at Peniel, 'I have seen God face to face, and yet my life is preserved,' is the counter-instance that John's absolute 'no one has seen God' engages and qualifies. The tradition of the perilous, near-impossible vision of God lies behind John's denial of any direct sight of God.

echoes.text: Yahweh appeared of old to me, saying, Yes, I have loved you with an everlasting love: therefore with loving kindness have I drawn you.
echoes.note: 'I have loved you with an everlasting love; therefore with lovingkindness have I drawn you' parallels John's account of love revealed and originating in God. The everlasting, drawing love of the LORD in Jeremiah anticipates the divine love manifested in the sending of the Son.

echoes.text: For you love all things that are, And abhor none of the things which you did make; For never would you have formed anything if you did hate it.
echoes.note: 'You love all things that exist... for you would not have made anything if you had hated it' offers a deuterocanonical precedent for predicating love of God's very relation to creation. This anticipates John's bolder 'God is love.'

echoes.text: Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth,
echoes.note: The summary confession 'God is love' (repeated) again distills the LORD's self-naming as abounding in steadfast love. John makes the Sinai attribute the definitive predicate of the divine being in which the believer abides.

echoes.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions. And also on the servants and on the handmaids in those days, I will pour out my Spirit.
echoes.note: 'Because he has given us of his Spirit' echoes the promise that God will pour out his Spirit on all flesh as the sign of his abiding presence in the last days. John reads the gift of the Spirit as evidence that believers remain in God and God in them.

echoes.text: I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.
echoes.note: 'I will put my Spirit within you and cause you to walk in my statutes' grounds John's claim that we know we abide in God 'because he has given us of his Spirit.' The indwelling Spirit as token of covenant intimacy underlies the Johannine mutual-abiding language.

echoes.text: “You are my witnesses,” says Yahweh, “With my servant whom I have chosen; that you may know and believe me, and understand that I am he. Before me there was no God formed, neither will there be after me. I myself am Yahweh; and besides me there is no savior. I have declared, I have saved, and I have shown; and there was no strange god among you. Therefore you are my witnesses”, says Yahweh, “and I am God.
echoes.note: 'We have seen and testify' echoes the LORD's appointment of Israel as witnesses ('you are my witnesses... that I am God'). The covenantal vocation to testify to the one God shapes John's testimony that the Father sent the Son as Savior of the world.

echoes.text: Declare and present it. Yes, let them take counsel together. Who has shown this from ancient time? Who has declared it of old? Haven’t I, Yahweh? There is no other God besides me, a just God and a Savior; There is no one besides me. “Look to me, and be saved, all the ends of the earth; for I am God, and there is no other.
echoes.note: 'The Savior of the world' draws on Isaiah's proclamation of the LORD as the only righteous God and Savior, to whom all the ends of the earth are summoned. John extends this universal salvific scope to the Son sent by the Father.

echoes.text: Yahweh didn’t set his love on you, nor choose you, because you were more in number than any people; for you were the fewest of all peoples: but because Yahweh loves you, and because he desires to keep the oath which he swore to your fathers, Yahweh has brought you out with a mighty hand, and redeemed you out of the house of bondage, from the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt.
echoes.note: 'We love him, because he first loved us' restates the Deuteronomic priority of divine election-love that precedes and grounds any human love for God. The prevenient love of the LORD setting his affection on Israel before any response is the template for John's 'he first loved us.'

echoes.text: “‘You shall not hate your brother in your heart. You shall surely rebuke your neighbor, and not bear sin because of him. “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: The charge against one who says 'I love God' yet hates his brother draws on the Holiness Code: 'you shall not hate your brother in your heart... you shall love your neighbor as yourself.' John binds love of God inseparably to love of the visible brother, fulfilling the neighbor command.

echoes.text: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.
echoes.note: 'He who loves God should also love his brother' joins the Shema's command to love God with the whole heart to neighbor-love as a single commandment 'we have from him.' John reads the love of God of the Shema as inseparable from the love of brother required by the Holiness Code.

echoes.text: The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge; but the foolish despise wisdom and instruction.
echoes.note: 'There is no fear in love; perfect love casts out fear' stands in deliberate tension with the wisdom maxim that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge. John transforms the servile fear of judgment into the boldness of perfected love, a development of the biblical fear-of-God tradition.

echoes.text: For wickedness, condemned by a witness within, is a coward thing, And, being pressed hard by conscience, always forecasts the worst lot: For fear is nothing else but a surrender of the help which reason offers;
echoes.note: 'For fear is nothing but a surrender of the helps that come from reason' provides a deuterocanonical reflection on fear as torment and bondage, paralleling John's 'fear has punishment.' The depiction of fear as inner anguish anticipating judgment resonates with John's contrast of fear and perfected love.

echoes.text: I said in my haste, “All men are liars.”
echoes.note: 'He is a liar' echoes the psalmist's 'all men are liars,' supplying the biblical category of the lie as a failure of covenant truthfulness. The brother-hater who claims love of God is exposed as a liar in the Johannine sense of one who does not do the truth.

echoes.text: “Thus has Yahweh of Armies spoken, saying, ‘Execute true judgment, and show kindness and compassion every man to his brother. Don’t oppress the widow, nor the fatherless, the foreigner, nor the poor; and let none of you devise evil against his brother in your heart.’
echoes.note: The prophetic insistence that true devotion to God is shown by mercy and not oppressing the brother resonates with John's argument that love of the unseen God must be embodied in love of the seen brother. Marked faint as a thematic rather than verbal parallel.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: You brought a vine out of Egypt. You drove out the nations, and planted it. You cleared the ground for it. It took deep root, and filled the land. The mountains were covered with its shadow. Its boughs were like God’s cedars. It sent out its branches to the sea, Its shoots to the River. Why have you broken down its walls, so that all those who pass by the way pluck it? The boar out of the wood ravages it. The wild animals of the field feed on it. Turn […]
echoes.note: The vine 'brought out of Egypt' that God planted and tended is the controlling image Jesus reworks: Israel-as-vine becomes Jesus the true vine. High volume and coherence — Ps 80 also has God's hand burning/cutting the vine (v.16), feeding the imagery of branches thrown into the fire in 15:6, and v.17 'the son of man' whom God strengthens.

echoes.text: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill. He dug it up, gathered out its stones, planted it with the choicest vine, built a tower in its midst, and also cut out a wine press therein. He looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes. “Now, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, please judge between me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my […]
echoes.note: The Song of the Vineyard: God's well-tended vineyard yields wild grapes and is judged. Jesus' 'true vine' answers Israel's failure to bear fruit; the Father as vinedresser (georgos) who prunes parallels the owner who tends and then strips Isaiah's vineyard. Strong thematic coherence on fruit-bearing and judgment.

echoes.text: Yet I had planted you a noble vine, wholly a right seed. How then have you turned into the degenerate branches of a foreign vine to me?
echoes.note: 'I planted you a choice vine... how then have you turned degenerate, a wild vine?' The contrast between the genuine (true) vine and the degenerate vine sharpens Jesus' 'I am the TRUE vine' — he is what planted Israel was meant to be. High coherence and availability.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s word came to me, saying, Son of man, what is the vine tree more than any tree, the vine-branch which is among the trees of the forest? Will wood be taken of it to make anything? Will men take a pin of it to hang any vessel on it? Behold, it is cast into the fire for fuel; the fire has devoured both its ends, and its midst is burned: is it profitable for any work? Behold, when it was whole, it was meet for no work: how much less, when the fire has […]
echoes.note: The vine-wood good for nothing but fuel, burned in the fire — directly underwrites 15:6, branches gathered, cast into fire, and burned. Ezekiel says the unfruitful vine is given to the fire for fuel; the verbal/conceptual link to the withered branch burned is strong.

echoes.text: He took also of the seed of the land, and planted it in a fruitful soil; he placed it beside many waters; he set it as a willow tree. It grew, and became a spreading vine of low stature, whose branches turned toward him, and its roots were under him: so it became a vine, and produced branches, and shot out sprigs. There was also another great eagle with great wings and many feathers: and behold, this vine bent its roots toward him, and shot out its […]
echoes.note: The vine planted and tended, which will or won't flourish and may wither, contributes to the cluster of prophetic vine imagery of planting, pruning and withering behind 15:1-6. Recurrence within the vine-of-Israel tradition strengthens it even though no single verbal quotation.

echoes.text: Your mother was like a vine, in your blood, planted by the waters: it was fruitful and full of branches by reason of many waters. It had strong rods for the scepters of those who bore rule, and their stature was exalted among the thick boughs, and they were seen in their height with the multitude of their branches. But it was plucked up in fury, it was cast down to the ground, and the east wind dried up its fruit: its strong rods were broken off and […]
echoes.note: Israel as a fruitful vine plucked up in fury, withered, and consumed by fire — same fruit/wither/fire complex as 15:2,6. Part of the recurrent Ezekiel vine-judgment tradition Jesus inverts as the true vine that abides.

echoes.text: Israel is a luxuriant vine that produces his fruit. According to the abundance of his fruit he has multiplied his altars. As their land has prospered, they have adorned their sacred stones.
echoes.note: 'Israel is a luxuriant vine that yields its fruit' yet turns to idolatry. Reinforces the vine-of-Israel topos of fruit that should but fails to glorify God, the backdrop for the true vine bearing 'much fruit' to the Father's glory (15:8).

echoes.text: He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither. Whatever he does shall prosper.
echoes.note: The righteous as a tree planted by water 'that yields its fruit in its season' and does not wither frames the abiding/fruit-bearing/withering antithesis of 15:2-6. Coherence with the abide-and-bear-fruit motif; tree rather than vine, so a softer echo.

echoes.text: Blessed is the man who trusts in Yahweh, and whose trust Yahweh is. For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters, who spreads out its roots by the river, and shall not fear when heat comes, but its leaf shall be green; and shall not be careful in the year of drought, neither shall cease from yielding fruit.
echoes.note: The one who trusts the Lord is like a tree planted by water that does not cease to bear fruit even in drought. Parallels remaining/abiding and continual fruit-bearing of the abiding branch (15:4-5); shares the 'not wither / bears fruit' contrast.

echoes.text: In that day, sing to her, “A pleasant vineyard! I, Yahweh, am its keeper. I will water it every moment. Lest anyone damage it, I will keep it night and day. Wrath is not in me, but if I should find briers and thorns, I would do battle! I would march on them and I would burn them together. Or else let him take hold of my strength, that he may make peace with me. Let him make peace with me.” In days to come, Jacob will take root. Israel will blossom and […]
echoes.note: The restored 'pleasant vineyard' that God keeps and waters night and day so Jacob 'shall fill the whole world with fruit' — the eschatological reversal of Isa 5. Jesus the true vine realizes this fruitful vineyard; coherence with 15:8's much fruit and the keeping/tending Father.

echoes.text: Binding his foal to the vine, his donkey’s colt to the choice vine; he has washed his garments in wine, his robes in the blood of grapes.
echoes.note: Judah's blessing binds the foal 'to the vine, his donkey's colt to the choice vine,' a messianic vine image read of the coming ruler. A faint contributory resonance to messianic 'true vine' typology rather than a direct source.

echoes.text: As the vine I put forth grace; And my flowers are the fruit of glory and riches.
echoes.note: Wisdom says 'I spread out my branches like a terebinth... like a vine I caused loveliness to bud, and my blossoms became glorious and abundant fruit.' Personified Wisdom as a fruitful vine offers a Second-Temple analogue to the 'I am the vine' self-predication, supporting the figural reading.

registers.label: Spare
lines: I am the vine; you are the branches.
Apart from him we can do nothing.
Abide in me, and I in you, he says.
And we will bear much fruit.
The Father prunes us that we may grow.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
Come, let us abide in the living Vine.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Come close to the Vine, you branches, you who feel cut back and bare this season.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
The sap that rises in him rises in you; abide there, and the leaves will come, and after the leaves the fruit.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
The Gardener's knife is not cruelty but care, clearing away what cannot bear so that you can.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
Stay rooted in his love, and your life will hang heavy with good fruit, like grapes in the warm of autumn.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!

lines: I am the vine; you are the branches.

We will bear good fruit. Alleluia!
